pl-l4d10c1-d1e115.summary: Describes others, going beyond the earlier error, who measure God's power by natural things and contradict the truth more boldly, saying Christ's body and blood are not on the altar and that bread and wine are not converted into the substance of flesh and blood; Christ said 'this is my body' as Paul said 'the rock was Christ', so that the body is there only in sacrament, that is, in sign, and eaten only in sign.
claims: Some deny that Christ's body is on the altar and hold it present only in sign.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e121.summary: Notes that they take occasion from Christ's words, from which the first heresy arose among his disciples: hearing 'unless one eats my flesh', some found it hard and left. Christ told the twelve that the spirit gives life and the flesh profits nothing, and Augustine glosses: understand spiritually; you will not eat this body you see or drink the blood those who crucify me will shed; I have commended a sacrament to you which, spiritually understood, will give you life.
claims: The heretics rely on John 6 and Augustine's spiritual reading.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e127.summary: Notes that there are other texts feeding their madness.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e131.summary: Gives one: Augustine says the Lord is above until the world ends, yet his truth is with us; the body in which he rose must be in one place, while his truth is diffused everywhere.
claims: Christ's risen body is in one place.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e140.summary: Gives another: God and man is one person, everywhere as God, in heaven as man.
claims: Christ is in heaven as man.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e146.summary: Gives Christ's saying: 'the poor you will always have with you, but me you will not always have'.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e149.summary: Notes that the heretics use these and other texts to assert their error.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e152.summary: Answers that all must be taken in the same sense: they do not deny that the faithful receive Christ's true body or that it is on the altar, but teach that his body is given not torn into parts, as the departing disciples thought, but whole; not visibly in human form, but invisibly under the form of bread and wine.
claims: The texts deny a divided or visible presence, not the true body.
Christ's body is given whole and invisibly under bread and wine.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e155.summary: Quotes Augustine confirming this: the same and not the same body that was seen is eaten: the same invisibly, not the same visibly.
claims: The same body is eaten invisibly, not visibly.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e165.summary: Adds Augustine: though it must be celebrated visibly, it must be understood invisibly.
claims: The sacrament is celebrated visibly and understood invisibly.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e171.summary: Interprets the claim that Christ's body is in one place: visibly in human form; his truth, the divinity, is everywhere, and his truth, the true body, is on every altar where it is celebrated.
claims: Christ's body is visibly in one place but truly on every altar.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e174.summary: Interprets 'me you will not always have' as referring to the bodily presence with which he lived among them.
claims: Christ's saying concerns his visible bodily presence.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e177.summary: Interprets 'in heaven as man': visibly; invisibly he is on the altar, not appearing in human form but covered by the form of bread and wine. So his flesh, truly on the altar, is called invisible, since it does not appear in its own species.
claims: Christ is visibly in heaven and invisibly on the altar.
His flesh on the altar is called invisible because it does not appear in its own form.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e180.summary: Quotes Augustine: the Church's sacrifice is made and consists of two things, the visible species of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of Christ, sacrament and reality of the sacrament, as Christ's person consists of God and man; everything contains the nature and truth of what it is made from. So the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament are the same body of Christ.
claims: The Church's sacrifice consists of visible species and Christ's invisible flesh.
This is compared to Christ's person composed of God and man.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e189.summary: Draws out that Augustine called Christ's flesh invisible because it is received and handled covered by the form of bread, and said the same body is sacrament and reality, confirming what was said.
claims: Christ's body is called invisible because it is hidden by the species.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e193.summary: Gives a more troubling passage of Augustine: it is his flesh we receive covered by the form of bread, and his blood we drink under the species and taste of wine; flesh is the sacrament of flesh and blood of blood; by flesh and blood, both invisible, intelligible, spiritual, Christ's visible and palpable body, full of grace and majesty, is signified.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e199.summary: Explains that Augustine uses a trope by which signifying things take the names of what they signify: the visible species of bread is called flesh and that of wine blood. Christ's flesh is called invisible and intelligible because under that species it is not seen as flesh but understood. The 'invisible flesh', the species under which Christ's flesh is not seen, is the sacrament of the visible flesh, signifying Christ's body which is visible and palpable where it appears in its own form; likewise for the blood.
claims: Augustine names the sign by what it signifies.
The species are the sacrament of Christ's visible body.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e205.summary: Adds that Augustine confirms this by explaining his obscure words: the bread is called Christ's body, while truly being the sacrament of Christ's body hung on the cross, as the immolation done by the priest's hands is called Christ's passion, not in reality but in signifying mystery, and as the sacrament of faith is called faith.
claims: The sacrament is called by the name of what it signifies.
The priest's offering is called Christ's passion as a signifying mystery.

pl-l4d10c1-d1e217.summary: Concludes that the heretics' objections have been answered: those who deny that Christ's true body is on the altar and that bread is converted into body and wine into blood by mystical consecration, asking who would dare eat his Lord or say that Christ's body is formed daily from matter that was not the Virgin's flesh.
claims: The objections against the true body on the altar are answered.

pl-l4d10c1.summary: Refutes those who, measuring God's power by natural things, deny that Christ's body and blood are on the altar or that bread and wine are converted into them, holding that 'this is my body' is said as 'the rock was Christ', a body only in sign. They draw on Christ's 'the spirit gives life, the flesh profits nothing', read with Augustine, and on texts that Christ's body is in one place, in heaven, and that 'you will not always have me'. Lombard answers that these texts deny not the true body on the altar but that it is given torn in pieces or visibly in human form: it is given whole and invisibly under bread and wine. Christ's body is visibly in one place in human form, but truly on every altar. Augustine's description of the flesh as 'invisible' and of the species as 'flesh' uses a trope, the sign taking the name of the thing signified, as the priest's offering is called Christ's passion. This suffices against those who ask who would dare eat his Lord, or how Christ's body could be formed daily from matter other than the Virgin's flesh.
claims: Some deny that Christ's body is on the altar and say it is present only in sign.
The texts they cite deny only a divided or visible presence.
Christ's body is given whole and invisibly under bread and wine.
Christ's body is visible in one place in heaven, but truly on every altar.
Augustine sometimes calls the sign by the name of the thing signified.
